Abstract
Automated Essay Scoring (AES) for Korean texts faces signiﬁcant challenges due to limited annotated
data and the morphological complexity of the Korean language. In this study, we apply and evaluate
two linguistically informed augmentation methods—BART-based CHEF and ELECTRA-based Random
Masking Insertion (RMI)—tailored to the characteristics of Korean. Additionally, we adopt a topic-aware
preprocessing strategy that embeds essay topics into model inputs to enhance topic awareness during train-
ing. Experiments on 44,658 Korean essays with 10-fold prompt-stratiﬁed cross-validation show that both
augmentation methods and topic-aware preprocessing yield statistically signiﬁcant improvements over a
KoBERT-based baseline (paired t-tests, all surviving a Holm correction), and that combining them raises
the quadratic weighted kappa (QWK) for the ﬁnal composite score from 0.4243 to 0.4360, with no signif-
icant degradation on any rubric item. To contextualize these scores, we recover the three raters’ original
scores and measure human agreement under the identical protocol. Model performance closely tracks the
human agreement proﬁle across rubric items (Spearman ρ = 0.82), and the headline QWK reaches 83%
of the human ceiling of 0.523, measured as the agreement of one rater with the average of the other
two—the same target the model predicts. These ﬁndings highlight the potential of linguistically informed
augmentation and topic-aware preprocessing in building robust Korean AES systems.
Keywords: automated essay scoring; text data augmentation; topic-aware preprocessing; korean morphemes; inter-annotator
agreement
1. Introduction
Recent educational reforms in South Korea have increasingly emphasized the cultivation of cre-
ativity and independent thinking among students. In alignment with these initiatives, national
assessment formats are undergoing a transition from conventional multiple-choice tests to more
expressive, open-ended formats such as narrative and essay-based evaluations. These formats are
designed to better assess students’ higher-order cognitive and interpretive abilities. However, the
inherently subjective nature of open-ended responses introduces challenges in achieving consis-
tency and reliability in scoring. In response, there has been a growing interest in developing AES
systems tailored to the Korean language.

A signiﬁcant milestone in this domain was the release of a large collection of annotated
essays—referred to as the Essay Writing Evaluation Dataa—by AI-HUBb, under the supervi-
sion of the National Information Society Agency (NIA). Although the ofﬁcial catalogue advertises
roughly 50,400 essays, the actually distributed raw data contains 45,497 labeled essays; after
removing duplicates, our study uses 44,658 essays (see Section 3 for the exact preprocessing
pipeline). This corpus has become a foundational resource for Korean AES research (Lee and
Kim 2023; Cho et al. 2021; Park and Lee 2022). Despite its contributions, the dataset remains
limited in scale for training robust neural models. Although it comprises 44,658 essays across 50
distinct prompts, each prompt includes only approximately 900 samples, resulting in sparse topic-
level representation. Furthermore, no comparable large-scale Korean essay dataset is currently
available, rendering data scarcity a signiﬁcant bottleneck for AES development.
Data augmentation presents a viable strategy to mitigate these limitations. However, its appli-
cation in the context of Korean AES remains relatively underexplored. Easy Data Augmentation
(EDA) (Wei and Zou 2019), one of the most widely adopted techniques in Korean NLP, consists of
four operations: synonym replacement (SR), random insertion (RI), random swap (RS), and ran-
dom deletion (RD). While EDA is computationally efﬁcient and easy to implement, it often fails
to preserve semantic and grammatical integrity, particularly in morphologically rich languages
such as Korean (Seo and Oh 2023). In particular, synonym replacement in EDA lacks contextual
sensitivity, frequently producing awkward or ungrammatical constructions due to disregard for
syntactic dependencies.
To address these shortcomings, several alternative approaches have been proposed. These
include embedding-based synonym replacement and Random Masking Replacement (RMR), in
which selected tokens are replaced with [MASK] tokens and subsequently predicted using a pre-
trained language model (Wu et al. 2019; Kobayashi 2018; Kim et al. 2020). Although these
methods exhibit improved contextual coherence compared to rule-based techniques, they still
encounter difﬁculties in handling Korean’s agglutinative morphology. Mismatches at the mor-
phological or syntactic level often lead to semantically or grammatically inappropriate outputs.
Moreover, the effectiveness of these methods in AES-speciﬁc contexts remains largely unveriﬁed,
as they have not been systematically evaluated within this domain.
More recently, large-scale language models (LLMs) have demonstrated considerable potential
for data augmentation in low-resource settings, including Korean AES. Among these, ChatGPT
has been the most studied; previous research (Kim and Park 2023) reported that ChatGPT-
generated text exhibits high semantic ﬁdelity and naturalness, as evidenced by cosine similarity
metrics and improvements in the performance of the AES model. Nevertheless, the high computa-
tional and ﬁnancial costs associated with API-based LLMs pose barriers to widespread adoption
in academic research. In contrast, open-source LLMs such as LLaMAc support local inference and
ﬁne-tuning, allowing for the development of augmentation strategies that are more linguistically
and appropriately tailored for the task. However, these models demand substantial computational
infrastructure, which may be inaccessible to smaller institutions. Consequently, while LLM-based
approaches are promising, their practical applicability in Korean AES is limited by both resource
and cost constraints. This underscores the need for augmentation methods that are computation-
ally efﬁcient, linguistically robust, and suitable for morphologically complex languages such as
Korean.
To address these challenges, the present study adapts and empirically evaluates two linguis-
tically informed data augmentation methods—CHEF and Random Masking Insertion (RMI)—
which, although previously proposed in Korean NLP literature, have not yet been applied to
AES tasks. Unlike LLM-based approaches, these methods leverage pretrained language models

(PLMs), offering a more computationally efﬁcient alternative that is better suited for resource-
constrained environments. Moreover, both CHEF and RMI are designed to preserve semantic
integrity while introducing meaningful linguistic variation. CHEF generates grammatically valid
and semantically coherent variants by decomposing and recombining lexical morphemes, thereby
leveraging the agglutinative nature of Korean (Seo et al. 2023). RMI extends the RMR approach
by inserting, rather than replacing, masked tokens, thereby preserving the original lexical context
while enabling controlled variation through masked language modeling (Yang 2022).
In addition, a topic-aware preprocessing strategy, inspired by prior work on prompt- and topic-
aware scoring (Gupta 2023; Cho et al. 2021; Jiang et al. 2023), is adopted. This approach involves
embedding prompt information into each sentence of an essay to improve topic sensitivity. Given
that the Essay Writing Evaluation Data comprises 50 distinct prompts—comparable in structure
to the ASAPd dataset used in English AES—the original prompt-insertion method is adapted to
account for the relatively short sentence lengths in Korean essays. In this modiﬁed version, each
sentence is explicitly labeled with the corresponding topic. We emphasize that topic-aware scoring
itself is an established technique; our contribution lies in its adaptation to a Korean AES model
and in a rigorous, statistically validated measurement of its effect.
Ultimately, the contributions of this study are summarized as follows:
1. We present the ﬁrst systematic application of two linguistically informed augmentation
techniques—CHEF and RMI—to Korean AES, together with a topic-aware preprocessing
strategy adapted to Korean (word-boundary insertion for RMI, sentence-level topic labeling).
2. We show that every proposed component yields a statistically signiﬁcant improvement over
the baseline: under 10-fold prompt-stratiﬁed cross-validation with paired t-tests, CHEF, RMI,
and topic-aware preprocessing each improve performance (p = 0.0044, 0.0106 and 0.0008;
all three survive a Holm correction over the ﬁve conﬁrmatory comparisons), with no signif-
icant degradation on any rubric item. Augmentation on top of topic-aware preprocessing is
positive in both cases and yields our best conﬁguration, but is nominally rather than adjusted-
signiﬁcant, and we report it as suggestive. As a supplementary comparison, we also situate the
baseline against the ofﬁcial word2vec-based reference models distributed with the corpus and
ﬁve traditional machine learning methods under the identical protocol.
3. We recover the three raters’ original scores and measure human agreement for all 11 rubric
items, under the same protocol used to score the model. The per-item performance proﬁle is
tightly aligned with human agreement (Spearman ρ = 0.82), and the composite-score QWK
of our best conﬁguration (0.4360) reaches 83% of the human ceiling of 0.523—the agreement
a single rater achieves with the average of the other two, which is precisely what the model is
asked to predict.
2. Related Work
This section reviews previous work across four areas: (1) Automated Essay Scoring, (2) Korean
Automated Essay Scoring, (3) general text data augmentation, and (4) Korean-speciﬁc text data
augmentation. Through this review, we situate the present study within the broader literature and
identify the relevance of adapting linguistically informed augmentation methods to Korean AES.
2.1 Automated Essay Scoring
AES has undergone signiﬁcant evolution over the past two decades. Early systems relied on sta-
tistical models with manually engineered features (Attali and Burstein 2006; Phandi et al. 2015).
Later, neural approaches using LSTM, CNN, and BiLSTM architectures enabled automatic feature

learning from raw text (Alikaniotis et al. 2016; Taghipour and Ng 2016; Dong and Zhang 2016).
The introduction of attention mechanisms and sentence-level representations further improved
models’ ability to capture discourse-level coherence (Dong et al. 2017; Dasgupta et al. 2018), and
several studies have modeled local coherence and discourse structure to enhance scoring ﬁdelity
(Farag et al. 2018; Tay et al. 2018; Li et al. 2018; Mesgar and Strube 2018). A recurring concern
throughout this progression is that neural scorers latch onto superﬁcial correlates of quality rather
than quality itself. Essay length is the standard example: it correlates strongly with human scores,
is trivial to compute, and a model that leans on it can post competitive agreement while being
blind to content. Jeon and Strube (2021) therefore proposed scoring from content representations
that are explicitly decorrelated from such surface cues. This concern is directly relevant to the
present work, because the corpus we use exhibits precisely this correlation between length and
school level (Section 3.1), and because two of its rubric items reward length and sentence form
explicitly.
Trait-based scoring—predicting the individual rubric dimensions rather than a single holistic
score, as we do here—forms a second relevant strand. Ridley et al. (2021) introduced a multi-task
model in which a trait-attention mechanism lets each trait attend to different parts of the essay
while sharing a common representation, reporting strong holistic and trait-level results on ASAP
and ASAP++e; Kumar et al. (2022) showed that a simpler multi-task BiLSTM can learn global
quality and ﬁne-grained traits jointly, at the cost of trait-speciﬁc modelling. Both ﬁndings motivate
our choice to predict all 11 rubric items from a single shared essay representation with one output
unit per item.
More recently, pre-trained language models (PLMs) such as BERT, XLNet, and Sentence-
BERT have been integrated into AES pipelines (Yang et al. 2020; Wang et al. 2022; Li et al. 2023),
alongside hybrid models that combine neural representations with hand-crafted features (Uto et al.
2020) and contrastive learning approaches (Xie et al. 2022). With the emergence of large language
models (LLMs) like GPT-4 and ChatGPT, the AES landscape has broadened to include feedback
generation (Stahl et al. 2024), second-language writing assessment (Yancey et al. 2023), human-
AI collaborative scoring (Xiao et al. 2025), and interpretable zero-shot trait-level scoring (Lee
et al. 2024).
Of particular relevance to this study is the line of work on prompt- and topic-aware scor-
ing. Jiang et al. (2023) proposed disentangled representation learning to separate prompt-speciﬁc
and prompt-invariant components of essay representations, improving domain generalization
for prompt-aware scoring; Gupta (2023) showed that directly injecting prompt information into
model inputs improves AES performance. These studies establish that making the scoring model
aware of the prompt is beneﬁcial; our work adapts this idea to a Korean AES model whose
encoder is frozen—so that the prompt has to be supplied to the scoring module rather than to
the encoder—and quantiﬁes its contribution with formal signiﬁcance testing.
2.2 Korean Automated Essay Scoring
Early work in Korean AES emphasized rule-based NLP approaches tailored to Korean linguistic
characteristics such as free word order and frequent ellipsis. Noh et al. (2014) proposed a sentence-
level scoring system based on morphological, syntactic, and semantic role analyses. The release
of the Essay Writing Evaluation Dataset by AI-HUB in 2021 was a major milestone, enabling the
development of baseline models and spurring subsequent research. Recent studies have explored
a range of architectures and evaluation targets. For instance, Cho et al. (2021) employed KoBERT
and KoGPT2f to build topic-aware scoring models on this corpus, demonstrating that jointly
encoding the essay topic and text beneﬁts Korean AES; our topic-aware preprocessing builds on

this insight. GRU-based models have shown advantages over RNN and LSTM in both efﬁciency
and accuracy (Park and Lee 2022), while tree-based methods like Random Forests have been
valued for interpretability (im Park and ki Choi 2023). Advanced strategies, including structured
representation learning and explainable AI, have also gained traction. Lee and Kim (2023) incor-
porated argument structure information to enhance scoring precision, and Lee (2025) proposed
a hybrid model combining shallow linguistic features and semantic embeddings. The PASTA-I
model, based on ELECTRA, was designed for rubric-aligned scoring (Lee et al. 2023), and Im
and Lim (2024) evaluated ChatGPT-based AES in classroom settings.
A practical difﬁculty in this literature is that reported results are rarely directly comparable.
Studies based on the Essay Writing Evaluation Data differ in prediction targets (holistic total
score vs. individual rubric items), score scales and binning schemes, data subsets, and valida-
tion protocols, and several report accuracy- or correlation-based metrics rather than QWK. For
instance, Lee and Kim (2023) ﬁne-tune KLUE-RoBERTa on the argumentative subset of the cor-
pus (20,442 training essays) and report a total-score QWK of 0.543 for their baseline and 0.627
for their argument-structure-aware model, where the total score is the sum of the eleven 0–3 item
scores rounded to integers; Cho et al. (2021) instead frame the task as score-range classiﬁcation
and report accuracy. Neither setting is commensurable with our protocol, which uses the full cor-
pus, frozen-encoder features, and a quartile-binned weighted composite score. As a consequence,
no established QWK reference exists for the full corpus under a rubric-level protocol such as
ours. We therefore contextualize our results in two ways: (i) as a supplementary experiment, we
re-implement and evaluate, under an identical cross-validation protocol, the ofﬁcial word2vec-
based LSTM/GRU reference models distributed with the corpus, together with ﬁve traditional
machine learning methods (Section 5.3); and (ii) we measure the inter-annotator agreement of
the corpus itself to establish a human agreement reference that contextualizes attainable QWK
(Section 3.3). Despite these efforts, Korean AES still suffers from limited data resources. Most
datasets are narrow in scope or small in scale, constraining model robustness and generalizability.
This highlights the importance of exploring augmentation strategies suited to the morphological
and stylistic richness of Korean.
2.3 Text Data Augmentation
Text data augmentation (DA) has become increasingly important for NLP, particularly in low-
resource settings. Unlike continuous domains like computer vision, language’s discrete nature
makes it difﬁcult to modify text without distorting meaning (Li et al. 2022). The methods proposed
in response can be grouped by the mechanism through which they introduce variation, and the
trade-off each mechanism makes between diversity and ﬁdelity is what distinguishes them. Early
DA methods include synonym replacement using WordNet (Zhang et al. 2015; Wei and Zou 2019),
which swaps words for dictionary synonyms and therefore varies the surface form with no model
of the surrounding context, and embedding-based substitutions (Wang and Yang 2015), which
draw the replacement from the nearest neighbours of the original word in a distributional space
and so respect topical ﬁt but not syntactic agreement. More recent work has leveraged masked lan-
guage models like BERT for context-aware perturbation (Wu et al. 2019; Kobayashi 2018; Kumar
et al. 2020), in which a token is replaced by [MASK] and the model predicts a substitute conditioned
on the entire remaining sentence—removing the context-insensitivity of the two earlier fami-
lies at the cost of requiring a pretrained model—and back-translation for meaning preservation
(Sennrich et al. 2016), where a sentence is translated into a pivot language and back, producing a
ﬂuent paraphrase over whose content the practitioner has little control. Noising techniques such as
insertion, deletion, and swap (Wei and Zou 2019) provide lightweight alternatives that require no
model at all, but degrade grammaticality roughly in proportion to how much they perturb. Beyond
these, generative and self-training approaches synthesize new examples outright rather than edit-
ing existing ones: template- and rule-based sampling (Kang et al. 2018), conditional generation

tations across examples (Chen et al. 2020), and model-in-the-loop pair construction for sentence
encoders (Thakur et al. 2021). Most recently, LLMs enable instruction-driven generation (Li et al.
2024; Whitehouse et al. 2023), denoising (Ghosh et al. 2023), synthetic labeling (Xiao et al. 2023),
and teacher-student distillation pipelines (Khattab et al. 2024; Viswanathan et al. 2023), at corre-
spondingly higher computational or API cost. In the context of AES, DA has been used to mitigate
topic imbalance and data scarcity. For example, Jong et al. (2022) applied back-translation with
score adjustments, Park et al. (2022) proposed EssayGAN for score-controlled essay genera-
tion, topic-aware augmentation using BART summarization was introduced by Gupta (2023), and
rubric-speciﬁc augmentation has been studied by Yoo et al. (2025).
2.4 Korean Text Data Augmentation
In Korean NLP, DA has been explored to alleviate resource constraints. Early efforts adapted
English-based methods—EDA, Masked Language Modeling (MLM), and back-translation—to
Korean tasks (Vu et al. 2022; Kim et al. 2020; Seo and Oh 2023). Vu et al. (2022) showed per-
formance gains on STS and NLI tasks. Kim et al. (2020) used a BERT-based MLM to overcome
rule-based limitations, while Seo and Oh (2023) introduced label-preserving strategies such as
DA-SC (spelling correction), EDA-POS (POS-aware augmentation), and DA-cMLM (conditional
masking), which improved results on small datasets. Subsequent work tailored augmentation more
closely to Korean linguistic properties. Yang (2022) proposed Random Masking Replacement
(RMR) and Random Masking Insertion (RMI): rather than replacing existing tokens—which in
Korean frequently breaks morphological agreement between stems and particles—RMI inserts
[MASK] tokens at sampled positions and lets a masked language model generate contextually
appropriate insertions, preserving all original tokens. Their experiments showed that RMI bet-
ter preserves meaning while improving downstream performance. Seo et al. (2023) proposed
CHEF, which exploits Korean’s agglutinative morphology: a sentence is decomposed into lex-
ical morphemes (content words) and grammatical morphemes (particles and endings), and a
sequence-to-sequence blender is trained to reconstruct full sentences from the lexical morphemes
only, yielding stylistically diverse but semantically consistent variants. Kim and Park (2023)
explored using ChatGPT for Korean essay augmentation. The study found that generated texts
retained semantic ﬁdelity and reduced manual workload, offering a relatively efﬁcient alterna-
tive to human-authored data. However, reliance on API-based access limits its scalability and
cost-effectiveness in long-term academic settings.
While these studies highlight the potential of data augmentation tailored to Korean, their appli-
cation to complex tasks like AES remains limited. In particular, AES presents unique challenges
due to its linguistic complexity and topic sparsity, underscoring the need for empirical investi-
gations into how existing augmentation techniques can be effectively adapted to Korean-speciﬁc
contexts. The present study ﬁlls this gap by evaluating CHEF and RMI—the two methods above
that are explicitly designed around Korean morphology—on the largest public Korean essay
corpus with a statistically rigorous protocol.
3. Dataset
This section describes the corpus, its rubric structure, its descriptive statistics, and its annotation
quality. We present the dataset before the methodology so that the rubric structure referenced by
the model architecture and the evaluation protocol is established ﬁrst.

3.1 Corpus Description
We use the Essay Writing Evaluation Data, the largest publicly available Korean essay corpus
developed under the supervision of the National Information Society Agency (NIA). The dataset
contains essays written by students from grade 4 of elementary school to grade 12 of high school.
The exact size of this corpus has been reported inconsistently in the literature; for example, Misgna
et al. (2024) cite 50,413 essays, matching the ofﬁcial catalogue description of roughly 50,400.
However, the actually distributed raw data contains 45,497 essays with complete rubric annota-
tions. Starting from these 45,497 essays, we removed duplicate essays—pairs with identical essay
content, identiﬁed both by exact string matching and by a sentence-embedding cosine similarity of
1.0 (i.e., textually indistinguishable duplicates)—yielding the ﬁnal corpus of 44,658 essays used
throughout this study. Table 1 summarizes its composition.
Table 2 reports essay length statistics measured over the entire corpus. Average essay length
increases monotonically with school level (from 316.5 characters for elementary school to 646.5
for high school), indicating that length and grade level are strongly correlated. We return to the
implications of this correlation for potential length-based shortcut learning in Section 6.
3.2 Rubric Structure and the Final Composite Score
Each essay is scored on a 0–3 scale for 11 rubric items, which are grouped into three broader
categories: Expression, Organization, and Content. Table 3 describes the evaluation criteria for
each rubric item. These scores refer exclusively to the original essays, and were produced entirely
by the corpus distributors in 2021; we had no role in the annotation process. According to the
corpus documentation, the 50 prompts were designed in consultation with domain experts, each
essay was independently rated by three expert raters against the ofﬁcial rubric of eleven items,
and records with missing or corrupted annotations were removed before release; the distributed
label is the average of the three raters’ scores. Beyond this, the documentation discloses nei-
ther the raters’ professional qualiﬁcations and training, nor their compensation, nor any reliability
statistics. Because the annotation procedure therefore cannot be characterized from the documen-
tation alone, we measure its outcome directly: the raw distribution includes each of the three
raters’ individual item scores, from which we compute inter-annotator agreement for every rubric

sides become equal-frequency four-class labels before the quadratic weighted kappa is taken. In
cross-validation this is done inside each validation fold, using only that fold’s essays; no quantity
derived from the training folds enters the binning, and no quantity derived from the ground truth
is used to bin the predictions. The identical protocol is applied when measuring inter-annotator
agreement on the FCS in Section 3.3, so that model and human scores are directly comparable.

3.3 Annotation Quality: Inter-Annotator Agreement
Essay grading is known to vary substantially between (and even within) human raters, and the
reliability of the labels bounds what any model can achieve. To make this bound explicit, we
obtained the raters’ original scores from the distributed raw data, which contain the individual
rubric scores of the three raters (denoted a/b/c) for each essay. We veriﬁed the mapping against
our working corpus by essay identiﬁer: all 44,658 essays (100%) were matched, and the three-
rater average reproduces the distributed label exactly for all 11 items. We then computed the
inter-annotator agreement (IAA) for each rubric item as the pairwise quadratic weighted kappa
(QWK)—the same metric used for model evaluation—over the full corpus.
Pairwise agreement alone, however, is not the quantity a model should be compared against.
The model predicts the average of the three raters, a target whose noise is reduced by averaging,
whereas a pairwise kappa compares one individual rater with another. To place a human rater on
exactly the same footing as the model, we additionally report a leave-one-out (LOO) agreement:
for each rater in turn, we score that rater’s judgments against the average of the remaining two,
under the identical protocol used for the model (per item, both sides rounded; at the composite
level, quartile binning as in Section 3.2). The LOO value is the matched human reference; the
pairwise value is reported alongside it because it is the quantity conventionally called IAA.

4.2 Data Augmentation
This section introduces the data augmentation strategies employed in this study to address the lim-
ited availability of Korean essay data and enhance model generalization. Given the importance of
preserving semantic integrity and lexical consistency in automated essay scoring, particular care
was taken in selecting augmentation methods suitable for the linguistic characteristics of Korean.
Speciﬁcally, two techniques—CHEF and RMI—were adopted, both of which are designed to
minimize distortion while increasing data diversity in an efﬁcient manner. Both methods are label-
preserving: every augmented essay inherits the rubric scores of its source essay, and no additional
human scoring is performed. Both methods also operate under pre-speciﬁed automatic ﬁltering
rules that discard degenerate generator outputs—for example, generations that are drastically trun-
cated relative to the source sentence are rejected and the original sentence is retained. The exact
criteria and thresholds are stated in Section 5.1. The semantic ﬁdelity of both methods is veri-
ﬁed quantitatively in Section 5.2 before being applied to the AES task. The following subsections
provide detailed descriptions of each method.
4.2.1 BART-based CHEF: Morphology-Aware Augmentation
This study adopts the data augmentation framework proposed in Seo et al. (2023), termed CHEF,
to generate linguistically valid sentence variants that reﬂect the agglutinative structure of Korean.
CHEF leverages Korean’s morphological richness, where lexical and grammatical morphemes
are concatenated to form complex word units. For instance, the English sentence "I eat an apple"
corresponds to the Korean sentence "나는사과를먹는다". While the English sentence com-
prises four independent words, its Korean counterpart is composed of three surface forms, each
potentially containing multiple morphemes:
English:

Korean:

pragmatic functions in Korean sentence construction. Korean’s agglutinative structure enables

4.3 Topic-Aware Data Preprocessing
Essay scoring is inherently inﬂuenced by the relevance, coherence, and alignment of the essay
content to the given prompt or topic. As scoring rubrics in AES systems often include topical
relevance as an explicit criterion, enabling the model to account for prompt-speciﬁc information
can signiﬁcantly enhance its ability to evaluate essays more holistically and accurately. Prompt-
and topic-aware scoring is an established direction in AES: Gupta (2023) demonstrated that inte-
grating prompt information into model inputs substantially improves AES performance, Cho et al.
(2021) applied topic-aware scoring to Korean AES, and Jiang et al. (2023) studied prompt-aware
scoring from a domain-generalization perspective. Following the ﬁndings of Gupta (2023), we
implement a topic-aware preprocessing strategy designed to inject topic context at the sentence
level. This design choice aligns with our architecture, wherein KoBERT operates on sentence-
level inputs and independently encodes each sentence into contextual embeddings (as illustrated
in Figure 1). Given that KoBERT does not natively model inter-sentence dependencies, encoding
the prompt at the sentence level ensures that topic relevance is available to the model during each
inference step.

5. Experiments
This section presents a series of experiments designed to evaluate the effectiveness of the pro-
posed methods for enhancing Korean AES. Speciﬁcally, we investigate two main components: (1)
linguistically informed data augmentation, and (2) topic-aware preprocessing.
The experimental evaluation comprises four primary aspects:
1. Semantic Preservation: Assessing whether augmented data generated by CHEF and RMI
methods preserve the semantic integrity of the original texts.
2. Baseline Comparison: Situating the proposed baseline relative to the ofﬁcial reference mod-
els distributed with the corpus and traditional machine learning methods under an identical
protocol, before evaluating the proposed methods on top of it.
3. Model Performance: Evaluating the impact of the proposed augmentation techniques and
topic-aware preprocessing on AES accuracy, with formal statistical signiﬁcance testing for
every comparison and an analysis of sensitivity to the augmentation ratio.
4. Combined Effects: Formally testing whether augmentation provides additional gains on top
of topic-aware preprocessing.
5.1 Experimental Settings and Evaluation Metric
All experiments were conducted under consistent settings. The AES model was trained on an
NVIDIA RTX 3090 Ti GPU. Each sentence is encoded independently by the frozen KoBERT
with a maximum of 100 word-piece tokens, and the ﬁnal-layer [CLS] vector is taken as the 768-
dimensional sentence representation. An essay is thus a sequence of sentence vectors; sequences
are truncated or zero-padded to 128 sentences, in both cases at the front (“pre” mode), so that the
last position always holds the ﬁnal sentence of the essay. The scoring module consists of a 3-layer
GRU (hidden sizes 256→128→64) with dropout 0.4 applied to the input of each layer; the essay
representation is the ﬁnal hidden state of the third layer, which the pre-padding convention makes
the state after the last real sentence. It passes through dropout 0.5 into a dense output layer with 11
sigmoid units. Training uses Adam with a learning rate of 5 × 10−4, decayed by exp(0.1(10 −e))
after epoch e = 10, a batch size of 64, MSE loss, at most 50 epochs, and a ﬁxed random seed of
42.
Augmentation generation settings. The augmented sets are produced once, with a ﬁxed seed
of 42, under the following criteria. For CHEF, the mBART-50 morpheme blender is ﬁne-tuned for
three epochs as described in Section 4.2, and a length-preservation rule is applied to its output: a
blended sentence whose word count falls below 80% of its source sentence is discarded and the
source sentence is retained in its place, so that a degenerate, heavily truncated blend can never
replace the original. For RMI, the insertion ratio is r = 0.30, giving ⌊n · r⌋inserted masks per
sentence as deﬁned in Equation 10; each mask is ﬁlled with a token sampled from the ten highest-
scoring predictions of the KoELECTRA generator, and sentences of fewer than two words are
returned unchanged. These are the pre-speciﬁed ﬁltering rules referred to in Section 4.2; they are
applied uniformly to every generated sentence, not to a sampled subset.
For performance evaluation, we employ 10-fold cross-validation stratiﬁed by prompt, so that
all 50 prompts are proportionally represented in every fold. We choose this protocol for two rea-
sons: a 10-fold split maximizes the training data available per fold while still yielding enough folds
for stable estimates and paired signiﬁcance testing, and stratiﬁcation by prompt removes prompt-
distribution imbalance across folds—an important consideration given that each of the 50 prompts
contributes only about 900 essays. All reported values are means over the 10 folds accompanied
by the fold-level sample standard deviation (computed with n −1 in the denominator).

5.2 Semantic Preservation and Augmentation Quality Validation
Before we directly evaluate the impact of augmented data on AES performance, we conduct a
separate task-speciﬁc evaluation to assess the semantic ﬁdelity of each augmentation method.
Rather than manually inspecting a small number of examples, our validation strategy combines (i)
pre-speciﬁed automatic ﬁltering rules applied uniformly to the entire generation pipeline, which
discard degenerate generator outputs before any augmented sentence enters the training data,
and (ii) the quantitative, corpus-wide evaluations described below. This ensures that every aug-
mented sentence—not merely a sampled subset—passes the same validity checks. We did not
perform exhaustive manual veriﬁcation of the augmented data, which we acknowledge as a limi-
tation; however, the two quantitative evaluations below directly measure the properties that manual
inspection would target (grammatical validity and meaning preservation) at the scale of the full
dataset.
To this end, we utilize the KLUE-STS dataset, a standard benchmark for sentence-level seman-
tic similarity in Korean. KLUE-STS is part of the Korean Language Understanding Evaluation
(KLUE) benchmark (Park et al. 2021), which is designed to assess various core NLP capabilities
across multiple tasks. The STS (Semantic Textual Similarity) component speciﬁcally measures
how well models capture the degree of semantic equivalence between two given sentences on
a continuous scale. We ﬁrst train a baseline STS model using the original KLUE-STS train-
ing set and measure its performance on the ofﬁcial test set. We then apply each augmentation
technique—CHEF, RMI, EDA, and RMR—to expand the training data, retrain the model on each
augmented set, and compare the resulting STS performance. Since the STS task requires ﬁne-
grained semantic matching between sentence pairs, any degradation in model accuracy suggests
that the augmented data may have introduced semantic drift. Conversely, maintained or improved
performance indicates better semantic preservation. In addition to task-level evaluation, we also
compute cosine similarity between sentence embeddings of original–augmented pairs across the
KLUE-STS training set. This metric provides a direct, model-agnostic estimate of semantic close-
ness. Taken together, these two evaluations—STS performance and cosine similarity—offer both
functional and structural perspectives on how well each augmentation method preserves mean-
ing. This dual assessment serves as a prerequisite to ensure the semantic reliability of augmented
samples before applying them to the AES task.

outputs for students of the source essay’s grade—the two methods differ, and we quantify the
difference rather than assert it. For every original/augmented sentence pair in the corpus we tagged

the source, grouped into three classes: the 13 tags of Plex; adverbs, roots and interjections (MAG,
MAJ, XR, IC), which are content words that our lexical set does not cover; and function morphemes.

data-hungry of the ratios that work, doubling the training set rather than tripling or quadrupling it.
Ratios beyond 1.5 provide no additional beneﬁt, and at the highest ratio tested (2.5) the topic-
aware condition loses signiﬁcance for both methods—consistent with training data becoming
increasingly dominated by generator-introduced noise as the oversampling factor grows.
5.6 Discussion: Interpreting Absolute QWK Against Human Agreement
The absolute FCS QWK values reported above (0.42–0.44) may appear low compared to ﬁgures
around 0.8 sometimes reported in the AES literature. Two factors explain this gap. First, published
QWK values are generally not comparable across studies of this corpus: prediction targets, score
scales, binning schemes, and validation protocols differ substantially (Section 2.2), and QWK is
highly sensitive to the number of classes and their distribution. Second, and more fundamentally,
the annotation-quality analysis of Section 3.3 establishes what is attainable on this metric at all.
Under the identical FCS quartile-binning procedure, a human rater scored against the average
of the other two—the same target the model is evaluated against—reaches a QWK of 0.523. Our
baseline (0.4243) and best conﬁguration (0.4360) thus stand at 81% and 83% of the human ceiling
for this exact protocol. The absolute values are low because the ceiling itself is low, not because
the models fall far short of what human raters achieve; but they do fall short of it, and we do not
claim parity.
The analysis also reframes the per-rubric performance differences. The model’s per-item QWK
proﬁle tracks the human agreement proﬁle closely (Spearman ρ = 0.818 against the LOO refer-
ence; Pearson r = 0.951, inﬂated by the two-cluster structure of the items); the items on which
the model scores lowest (Novelty, 0.1428; Grammar, 0.2583) are precisely those on which human
raters disagree most (LOO agreement 0.295 and 0.387; Table 5), and on six items the model meets
or exceeds the agreement a human rater reaches with the average of the other two. This indicates
that the remaining errors on subjective items largely reﬂect label noise rather than correctable
model deﬁciencies. It is particularly noteworthy that the largest augmentation gains arise exactly
on Novelty, the noisiest item: augmentation appears to compensate for data scarcity where the
learning signal is weakest, although improvements on items with low human agreement should be
interpreted with additional caution, as QWK estimates are inherently noisier there. The composite-
level picture is different from the item-level one: there the model remains clearly below the human
ceiling (Section 3.3), and the gap of roughly 0.10 QWK is the margin that future work on this
corpus has to close.
6. Ethical Considerations
Automated essay scoring is a high-stakes application: the essays in our corpus were written by
students from grade 4 through grade 12, and scoring outcomes can inﬂuence the educational tra-
jectories of minors. We therefore discuss the ethical implications of this work and the precautions
we consider necessary for any deployment.
Human-in-the-loop deployment. Given the performance characteristics documented in this
paper, we do not consider fully automated, unassisted scoring to be an appropriate use of the
presented system. Its intended role is to support human raters—for example, as a second opinion,

a consistency check, or a triage mechanism that ﬂags essays for closer human review. Final scoring
authority in any consequential setting should remain with trained human raters.
Rubric-level reliability stratiﬁcation. The inter-annotator agreement analysis in Section 3.3
provides a principled basis for deciding which automated judgments can be trusted. Rubric items
with near-ceiling human agreement and model performance (Sentence, Length, In-paragraph,
Prompt; QWK ≥0.91) are plausible candidates for automated assistance. Conversely, for subjec-
tive items with low human agreement (Novelty, IAA 0.284; Clarity, 0.339; Descriptions, 0.364),
neither human nor model scores are reliable in isolation; automated scores on these items should
be presented with explicit uncertainty indications, if at all, and should never be used as the sole
basis for feedback or grading. Communicating this stratiﬁcation to teachers and students is, in our
view, a precondition for responsible use.
Fairness and shortcut risks. Essay length is strongly correlated with school level in this corpus
(Section 3.1), and length-related rubric items are among the easiest to predict. This creates a risk
that models exploit length as a shortcut, potentially disadvantaging concise writers or students
whose length norms differ from their cohort. Deployments should monitor performance separately
across school levels and demographic groups where lawful and appropriate, and should audit for
length-driven scoring artifacts.
Data privacy. All experiments use the Essay Writing Evaluation Data, which was collected,
de-identiﬁed, and publicly released by the National Information Society Agency (NIA) through
AI-HUB under its own consent and privacy framework. No new personal data were collected for
this study, and augmented essays are derived exclusively from the de-identiﬁed public corpus.
Explainability. The system presented here produces a number for each rubric item and no
account of it: the essay is represented as a sequence of frozen sentence embeddings compressed
by a GRU, and nothing in the architecture identiﬁes which passage of an essay drove a given
score. For a scoring decision that a student may wish to contest, this is a substantive shortcom-
ing, and it is a second reason—alongside the reliability limits above—to restrict the system to a
human-assisted role. Interpretable scoring has been pursued in the Korean AES literature through
rubric-aligned models and tree-based scorers whose features can be inspected (Lee et al. 2023;
im Park and ki Choi 2023), and more recently through LLM-based trait-level scoring that emits a
rationale alongside the score (Lee et al. 2024). Predicting all eleven criteria separately, as we do,
is a partial step in this direction—a per-criterion score is more actionable to a teacher than a single
holistic number, and the stratiﬁcation above indicates which of those criteria to trust—but it is
not an explanation. Combining linguistically informed augmentation with an explicit explanation
mechanism is, in our view, the most valuable direction for making systems of this kind deployable
in classrooms, and we leave it to future work.
Transparency and reproducibility. To support scrutiny of the claims made here, we report
exact dataset construction steps, fold splits, statistical procedures, augmentation ﬁltering criteria,
and rubric weights in full. We believe such transparency is particularly important for systems that
may inform the assessment of students.
7. Conclusion
This study advances automated essay scoring for the Korean language by systematically evalu-
ating two linguistically informed data augmentation techniques—CHEF and Random Masking
Insertion—together with a topic-aware preprocessing strategy, under a statistically rigorous pro-
tocol. Using 10-fold prompt-stratiﬁed cross-validation with paired signiﬁcance tests on 44,658
essays, we showed that CHEF (1:1) and RMI (r = 0.3, 1:1) each signiﬁcantly improve scoring
performance and that topic-aware preprocessing contributes an independent signiﬁcant gain, all
three surviving a multiplicity correction. Augmentation applied on top of topic-aware preprocess-
ing improves the composite-score QWK further, from 0.4243 to 0.4360 for the best conﬁguration

rather than adjusted-signiﬁcant and we treat it as suggestive. The gains concentrate on the most
difﬁcult content criteria, most notably novelty, where the baseline is weakest.
Beyond these performance results, this study contributes an empirical characterization of the
corpus itself. By recovering the three raters’ original scores, we quantiﬁed human agreement for
every rubric item under the protocol used to score the model, comparing each rater against the
average of the other two—the same target the model predicts. The model’s per-item performance
proﬁle closely tracks this proﬁle (Spearman ρ = 0.82), and the composite-score human ceiling
is 0.523. This analysis (Section 5.6) reframes absolute QWK values on this corpus: values near
0.43 are not evidence of a weak model but of a metric whose human ceiling is itself close to
0.5, although the model does remain measurably below that ceiling, and the remaining errors
on subjective items largely reﬂect annotation noise rather than correctable model deﬁciencies. A
supplementary comparison with the ofﬁcial word2vec-based reference models distributed with
the corpus and ﬁve traditional machine learning methods provides additional reference points for
these results.
A ratio-sensitivity analysis over ﬁve augmentation levels (Section 5.5) conﬁrmed that this 1:1
conﬁguration—for both CHEF and RMI (r = 0.3)—is not an arbitrary choice: gains are non-
monotonic in the ratio, a 0.5:1 ratio is insufﬁcient in three of the four settings tested and unstable
in the fourth, and ratios beyond 1.5:1 provide no further beneﬁt. Ratio 1.0 is in fact the only
level at which every method and condition improves signiﬁcantly and no rubric item degrades,
so the simplest conﬁguration that avoids oversampling the training set is also the most reliable
one, providing practical guidance for future Korean AES development. Future research directions
include exploring adaptive augmentation strategies responsive to speciﬁc prompts or rubric items,
integrating more advanced pre-trained language models, obtaining human judgments of grade-
level plausibility for augmented text, and developing ensemble approaches to further boost AES
performance. We hope that the combination of linguistically grounded augmentation, topic-aware
preprocessing, and annotation-aware evaluation presented here provides a solid and transparent
foundation for subsequent work on Korean AES.
